summary.text: Rewrite the ratio as \((\zeta(n)^2-\zeta(2n))/(\zeta(n)^2+\zeta(2n))\), and truncate the two Dirichlet series at denominator \(10\), whose tails are \(O(11^{-n})\). An exact polynomial cancellation after subtracting the four leading terms leaves only monomials with effective denominator at least \(11\), and division preserves the bound because \(\zeta(n)^2+\zeta(2n)\to2\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 z_n=\zeta(n),\qquad w_n=\zeta(2n),\qquad
 t(n)=\frac{w_n}{z_n^2},
\]
where, for the positive integers under consideration, the zeta values are real. We prove that
\[
 \frac{1-t(n)}{1+t(n)}-
 \left(2^{-n}+3^{-n}+5^{-n}+7^{-n}\right)=O(11^{-n}).
\]
All assertions below are asymptotic as the integer variable \(n\to\infty\), so the finitely many values \(n\leq 1\), where the Dirichlet series for \(\zeta(n)\) is not available, are irrelevant.

We use the standard meaning of the big-O notation: \(f_n=O(g_n)\) means that there are constants \(C\) and \(N\) such that \(|f_n|\leq C|g_n|\) for every \(n\geq N\).

### 1. A uniform bound for Dirichlet-series tails

We first record a tail estimate that will be used twice. For positive integers \(m\) and integers \(n\geq2\), set
\[
 T_{m,n}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac1{(k+m)^n}.
\]
The series converges because it is a tail of a convergent \(p\)-series. More quantitatively, for each \(k\geq0\), both
\[
 m\leq k+m\quad\hbox{and}\quad k+1\leq k+m.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 m^{n-2}(k+1)^2\leq(k+m)^n,
\]
and hence
\[
 \frac1{(k+m)^n}
 \leq \frac1{m^{n-2}(k+1)^2}
 =m^2m^{-n}\frac1{(k+1)^2}.
\]
Summing this inequality gives
\[
 0\leq T_{m,n}\leq C_m m^{-n},
 \qquad
 C_m:=m^2\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac1{(k+1)^2}<\infty. \tag{1}
\]
If \(m\geq11\), then \(m^{-n}\leq11^{-n}\), so (1) implies
\[
 T_{m,n}=O(11^{-n}). \tag{2}
\]
We will particularly use this with \(m=11\).

For every integer \(n>1\), the Dirichlet-series representation of the Riemann zeta function gives
\[
 \zeta(n)=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}r^{-n}
 =1+\sum_{r=2}^{\infty}r^{-n}. \tag{3}
\]
The complex formulation causes no issue here: every summand in (3) is real, so the real part of the complex zeta value equals the real series displayed above.

Define the three finite sums
\[
 S_n=2^{-n}+3^{-n}+5^{-n}+7^{-n}, \tag{4}
\]
\[
 U_n=2^{-n}+3^{-n}+4^{-n}+5^{-n}+6^{-n}
       +7^{-n}+8^{-n}+9^{-n}+10^{-n}, \tag{5}
\]
and
\[
 V_n=U_{2n}. \tag{6}
\]
Splitting (3) after the term \(10^{-n}\), we obtain, for \(n>1\),
\[
 z_n=1+U_n+e_n,
 \qquad e_n:=\sum_{r=11}^{\infty}r^{-n}. \tag{7}
\]
By (2),
\[
 e_n=O(11^{-n}). \tag{8}
\]
Likewise, applying the same splitting to \(\zeta(2n)\),
\[
 w_n=1+V_n+f_n,
 \qquad f_n:=\sum_{r=11}^{\infty}r^{-2n}. \tag{9}
\]
Estimate (1), with exponent \(2n\), gives
\[
 0\leq f_n\leq C_{11}11^{-2n}\leq C_{11}11^{-n},
\]
so
\[
 f_n=O(11^{-n}). \tag{10}
\]

For every integer \(b>1\), \(b^{-n}=(1/b)^n\to0\). It follows from (4)--(6), each of which is a finite sum, that
\[
 S_n\to0,
 \qquad U_n\to0,
 \qquad V_n\to0. \tag{11}
\]
Equations (7)--(10) therefore also show
\[
 z_n\to1,
 \qquad w_n\to1. \tag{12}
\]
In particular, all of \(S_n\), \(z_n\), \(1+U_n\), and their finite sums and products are bounded for sufficiently large \(n\).

### 2. The finite algebraic cancellation

The reason the four terms in \(S_n\) give the approximation through order \(11^{-n}\) is an exact finite cancellation. Put
\[
 a=2^{-n},\qquad b=3^{-n},\qquad c=5^{-n},\qquad d=7^{-n}.
\]
Using multiplicativity of integer powers, (4)--(6) become
\[
 S_n=a+b+c+d, \tag{13}
\]
\[
 U_n=a+b+a^2+c+ab+d+a^3+b^2+ac, \tag{14}
\]
and
\[
 V_n=a^2+b^2+a^4+c^2+a^2b^2+d^2+a^6+b^4+a^2c^2. \tag{15}
\]
Consider the finite expression
\[
 P_n=(1+U_n)^2-(1+V_n)
       -S_n\bigl((1+U_n)^2+(1+V_n)\bigr). \tag{16}
\]
We claim that
\[
 P_n=O(11^{-n}). \tag{17}
\]

To prove this without hiding the relevant cancellation, assign to a monomial
\(a^ib^jc^kd^\ell\) its base
\[
 q=2^i3^j5^k7^\ell.
\]
After substituting the definitions of \(a,b,c,d\), that monomial is exactly \(q^{-n}\). Thus any monomial whose base is at least \(11\) is individually \(O(11^{-n})\).

Rewrite (16) as
\[
 P_n=2(U_n-S_n)+(U_n^2-V_n)-2S_nU_n-S_n(U_n^2+V_n). \tag{18}
\]
There is no constant term. The only possible monomial bases below \(11\) are
\[
 2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10.
\]
The terms of bases \(2,3,5,7\) do not occur in (18): in its first summand they disappear in \(U_n-S_n\), and all the other summands have total degree at least two in \(a,b,c,d\).

It remains to inspect bases \(4,6,8,9,10\), represented respectively by
\[
 a^2,\quad ab,\quad a^3,\quad b^2,\quad ac.
\]
Their coefficients in the four summands on the right side of (18) are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrr|r}
\text{monomial}&2(U-S)&U^2-V&-2SU&-S(U^2+V)&\text{total}\\ \hline
 a^2&2&0&-2&0&0\\
 ab&2&2&-4&0&0\\
 a^3&2&2&-2&-2&0\\
 b^2&2&0&-2&0&0\\
 ac&2&2&-4&0&0
\end{array}
\]
Each entry follows immediately by multiplying the short sums (13)--(15). For example, the two contributions to \(a^3\) in \(-S(U^2+V)\) are \(-a\cdot a^2\) from \(-SU^2\) and \(-a\cdot a^2\) from \(-SV\), giving \(-2a^3\). This table accounts for every possible base below \(11\), and every total is zero.

Therefore, after expanding the finite polynomial (18), every surviving monomial has base \(q\geq11\). If the expansion is written as
\[
 P_n=\sum_{r=1}^{M}\lambda_r q_r^{-n},
 \qquad q_r\geq11,
\]
where \(M\) is finite and the \(\lambda_r\) are fixed real coefficients, then
\[
 |P_n|\leq\sum_{r=1}^{M}|\lambda_r|q_r^{-n}
 \leq\left(\sum_{r=1}^{M}|\lambda_r|\right)11^{-n}.
\]
This proves (17).

### 3. Replacing the finite approximations by the zeta values

Let
\[
 A_n=1+U_n,
 \qquad B_n=1+V_n.
\]
Equations (7)--(10) say
\[
 z_n-A_n=O(11^{-n}),
 \qquad w_n-B_n=O(11^{-n}). \tag{19}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
 z_n^2-A_n^2=(z_n-A_n)(z_n+A_n).
\]
By (11) and (12), \(z_n+A_n\to2\), and is therefore bounded. The first relation in (19) consequently gives
\[
 z_n^2-A_n^2=O(11^{-n}). \tag{20}
\]

Define the numerator
\[
 N_n=z_n^2-w_n-S_n(z_n^2+w_n). \tag{21}
\]
Subtracting (16) from (21) and collecting corresponding terms gives the exact identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
 N_n-P_n
   ={}&(z_n^2-A_n^2)-(w_n-B_n)\\
     &-S_n\bigl((z_n^2-A_n^2)+(w_n-B_n)\bigr). \tag{22}
\end{aligned}
\]
The first two differences on the right are \(O(11^{-n})\) by (19) and (20). Their sum is therefore \(O(11^{-n})\). Also, \(S_n\to0\), so \(S_n\) is bounded; multiplying an \(O(11^{-n})\) quantity by this bounded factor preserves the same big-O estimate. Thus (22) yields
\[
 N_n-P_n=O(11^{-n}).
\]
Combining this with (17), we conclude that
\[
 N_n=O(11^{-n}). \tag{23}
\]

### 4. Division by the denominator

Set
\[
 D_n=z_n^2+w_n.
\]
By (12),
\[
 D_n\longrightarrow1^2+1=2. \tag{24}
\]
Hence, for all sufficiently large \(n\), \(D_n\neq0\), and \(D_n^{-1}\) is bounded (for instance, eventually \(|D_n|\geq1\)). From (23) it follows that
\[
 \frac{N_n}{D_n}=O(11^{-n}). \tag{25}
\]
Similarly, (12) implies that \(z_n\neq0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), so the following algebraic manipulation is valid eventually. Since \(t(n)=w_n/z_n^2\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac{1-t(n)}{1+t(n)}-S_n
 &=\frac{1-w_n/z_n^2}{1+w_n/z_n^2}-S_n\\
 &=\frac{z_n^2-w_n}{z_n^2+w_n}-S_n\\
 &=\frac{z_n^2-w_n-S_n(z_n^2+w_n)}{z_n^2+w_n}\\
 &=\frac{N_n}{D_n}.
\end{aligned}
\]
By (25), the last expression is \(O(11^{-n})\). Recalling the definition (4) of \(S_n\), this is precisely
\[
 \frac{1-t(n)}{1+t(n)}
 =\frac1{2^n}+\frac1{3^n}+\frac1{5^n}+\frac1{7^n}
   +O\!\left(\frac1{11^n}\right),
\]
as claimed.
